title: Religious experience
note: The argument from religious experience treats apparent experiences of God like other perceptual experiences: they are evidence for what they seem to show unless there is reason to doubt them. Swinburne defends this with his principle of credulity, Alston by comparing mystical and sense perception. Critics point to conflicting experiences, missing public checks, and natural explanations.

read.title: Seeming and believing
text: Many people across history report experiences that seem to them to be awareness of God. Richard Swinburne argues that such reports are evidence, using a principle we apply everywhere else: the principle of credulity. If it seems to me that something is present, then probably it is, unless I have special reason to doubt it.

(1) If it seems to a person that x is present, then probably x is present, unless there is a defeater. (2) It seems to many people that God is present to them. (3) No defeater applies across the board to these experiences. (4) So probably God is present to them, and so God exists.
Swinburne adds a principle of testimony: other people's experiences are probably as they report them. So those without such experiences can also count them as evidence.

The best-known objection is from conflict. Christians report experiences of the Trinity, Hindus of Krishna, Buddhists of no personal God at all. If experiences support incompatible beliefs, perhaps none deserves trust.

Defenders reply that disagreement among witnesses usually calls for care, not wholesale dismissal. Many reports agree on a reality beyond the self that is holy and good. William Alston adds that sense perception also yields conflicting judgments and cannot be checked without relying on itself, yet we rightly trust it. Critics answer that sense perception has far more widely shared checks than religious perception does.

q.q: Which premise does the conflict objection mainly challenge?
What does the principle of testimony add?
o: Those without the experience can use others' reports as evidence
Testimony always outweighs one's own experience
Sense perception also faces conflict and circular checks, yet we trust it
Mystical perception is identical to sight
Religious experience needs no defense at all
